title: The ordeal bean becomes a drug

confidence.note: Christison's 1855 paper, Fraser's 1863 account of the ordeal and the later chemical and ophthalmic papers are all dated publications. The ordeal death toll is a missionary estimate and an Edinburgh physician's report, not a count.

people: Robert Christison, Edinburgh professor and toxicologist who ate part of a bean
Thomas R. Fraser, Edinburgh physician who described the ordeal and the bean's action
Ludwig Laqueur (1839–1909), ophthalmologist who introduced it for glaucoma
Percy Lavon Julian (1899–1975), chemist who synthesized physostigmine
summary: A poison used to try the accused in Old Calabar became, via a Scottish professor who ate one, a glaucoma drug and a landmark of chemistry.
body: In Old Calabar, in today's southeastern Nigeria, people accused of witchcraft or crimes were made to eat the seeds of a local vine, called *esere*: vomiting declared them innocent, death proved them guilty. Missionaries who arrived in 1846 estimated it killed some 120 people a year, and beans soon reached Scotland. In 1855 the Edinburgh toxicologist Robert Christison ate part of one and recorded the effects. Its alkaloid, physostigmine, was isolated in 1864, and from 1876 it was used to lower the pressure in eyes with glaucoma. In 1935 the Black chemist Percy Julian synthesized it.

title: A Caesarean section in Bunyoro

confidence.note: The operation is known only from Robert Felkin's own report, published five years later in an Edinburgh journal; no other witness or local record describes it. Later writers place it in the Bunyoro kingdom, while Felkin's phrasing, as quoted, speaks of 'Uganda'.

people: Robert W. Felkin (1853–1926), British medical student and eyewitness
An unnamed Banyoro healer and his assistants
summary: In 1879 a British medical student watched an African healer deliver a baby by Caesarean section, and saw the mother recover.
body: In 1879 Robert Felkin, a British medical student traveling with a missionary expedition, watched a healer at Kahura, in the kingdom of Bunyoro in western Uganda, deliver a baby by Caesarean section. The woman was sedated with banana wine, which was also used to wash her belly and the operator's hands; bleeding was seared with a red-hot iron, and the wound closed with seven iron pins. Felkin followed mother and child for 11 days and found the wound healed. His report, published in 1884, describes a practiced technique, yet it remains the only eyewitness account.

links.note: Another African practice reported by visiting Victorian doctors.
